GOAL: Build an inventory of every NUMERIC LIMIT OR DEFAULT that governs behavior, found under:
- guardrails/*.py and guardrails/*.sh (all check-*.py, check-*.sh scripts, and helper scripts like archformat.py, crosscut_counter.py, net_meter.py, node_growth_counter.py, nonempty_input.py, reap_owned_group.py, route_agent_transport.py, specformat.py, cleanup_notice.py, fence-refresh.sh)

- Also check any numeric threshold hardcoded directly in the .py/.sh scripts (e.g. line-count limits, retry counts, sleep/timeout values, percentage thresholds, "MAX_" constants).

For EACH numeric parameter you find, produce a row with these exact fields (pipe-delimited, one per line):
parameter | current value | exact source (path:line) | scope (what it governs, one phrase) | stated owner/origin (quote any comment in the file attributing the number, or "none stated") | evidence/rationale found (quote comment/docstring, or "none stated") | user-configurable? (yes/no/unclear + brief note) | override path (if stated, else "none stated")

ADDITIONALLY, for the 12-15 numbers that look most consequential (caps that would block a commit/PR, thresholds that gate CI) or most arbitrary/suspicious, run:
`git log -S"<the exact number>" --oneline -- <file>`
from within /Users/sashaabramovich/live-spec to find the introducing commit. Confirm with `git log -p -S"<number>" -- <file> | head -50` if ambiguous, and check the commit message via `git log -1 <sha>` or `git show --stat <sha>`. Record the SHA and whether the commit message states a rationale (quote it) or gives none.

Do not propose new values, do not judge whether numbers are good. Just report and cite.

Be thorough - this surface likely has 20-35+ distinct numeric parameters across the JSON configs and script constants. Sweep every JSON file listed and grep every .py/.sh file for integer literals in threshold-like contexts (comparisons like `> N`, `>= N`, `<= N`, `MAX =`, `LIMIT =`, `CAP =`, `.get("...", N)`, etc).

Report back ALL rows as your final message in the pipe-delimited format above, grouped by file. Do not truncate or summarize away rows — the full list is the deliverable.

- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts — when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, keeping state shared across viewers, handing the viewer a file to save, or updating and republishing itself. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review. For ultra on a GitHub.com PR target, --post asks to post the finished review’s findings to the PR as a single comment from the user’s GitHub account (not a review; the launch dialog still confirms in interactive sessions, while non-interactive mode posts on the flag alone) and --no-post hides that option.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

2	  "_comment": "The known-red proof for every gate guardrails/pre-push runs (SPEC INV-212, gate w). A gate that cannot red is a check that looks at nothing (the hollow authority-anchor gate this movement rebuilt, commit 8a0209f). check-every-gate-can-fail.py enumerates the `-- gate X:` markers pre-push invokes and requires each classified here: a `proof` names a red-first test `<file>::<function>` that drives the gate's check to a non-zero exit, tied to the gate by a `reds` token the proof file must reference (usually the check's basename); a `covered` entry names a gate that runs no independent check of its own and rides another gate's red, with the reason it holds no separate fixture. A proof is verified by structure (file exists, function defined, token present, a non-zero-exit assertion in the function body), since the suite runs it under gate b. A gate classified nowhere reds, a reasonless `covered` reds, a `cannot_red` gate reds loudly (a gate that can never fail is a finding, not a carve-out), and a key naming no local gate reds.",

2	  "_comment": "The tier-refusal data (ROADMAP row 507, the routing experiment opened 2026-07-28). A dispatch to the expensive tier proves its own need in three steps, and money is spent only on the middle one. Step one: `instruction` is the line a brief-writing session pastes verbatim into an expensive-tier brief, so the wording stays one text across every brief. Step two: a run that stops names a cheaper tier, and the orchestrator writes that refusal into `record` and re-runs the same brief a tier down. Step three: `patterns` holds the phrases learned from the record, and a phrase turns a task away before any model call. The list starts empty and grows from the record alone. guardrails/check-tier-refusal.py reads this file and the record together.",
3	
4	  "record": "docs/measure/tier-refusals.md",
5	
6	  "record_columns": ["Id", "Date", "Task", "Named tier", "Reason"],
7	  "_record_shape_comment": "One table row per refusal, appended, never edited afterwards. `Id` is a short label a pattern cites (TR-001, TR-002, …), unique within the record. `Date` is the day the refusal happened, written YYYY-MM-DD. `Task` is the brief's own words, trimmed to the sentence that says what the work is, so a phrase can be read out of it later. `Named tier` is the tier the run named, drawn from `tiers`. `Reason` is one sentence saying what makes the work fit that tier. A row missing its tier or its reason reds the gate, since a refusal that names neither teaches nothing.",
8	
9	  "tiers": ["haiku", "sonnet", "opus"],
10	  "_tiers_comment": "This host's tier ladder, cheapest first; the last member is the expensive tier the instruction is pasted into. A host with other names for its tiers edits this list, and the gate reads the names from here.",
11	
12	  "instruction": "Assume a cheaper tier does this task. Read the brief first: when a cheaper tier does it as briefed, stop before any other work and reply with one line — REFUSE <tier>: <one sentence of reason> — naming the tier that fits. Do the work when the brief needs the tier it was sent to.",
13	  "_instruction_comment": "The line opens the brief. It states the cheap tier as the default assumption, since a run judging its own need leans toward yes (the weakness row 507 states). The refusal costs the brief plus one short line. `REFUSE <tier>: <reason>` is the form the orchestrator reads a record row out of.",
14	
15	  "promotion": {
16	    "refusals_required": 3,
17	    "phrase_min_words": 2,
18	    "phrase_max_words": 8
19	  },
20	  "_promotion_comment": "How a phrase becomes a pattern. A phrase is a run of consecutive words copied out of a refused task's text, lowercased with punctuation dropped, between `phrase_min_words` and `phrase_max_words` long. It is promoted when `refusals_required` refusals in the record agree: each of them names the same tier, and each of their task texts carries the phrase word for word. The gate re-reads those refusals every run, so a pattern with fewer agreeing refusals behind it reds and a person reading a pattern here sees the three rows that put it there.",

The list is empty at the experiment's start, and the record is its only source."

=== check-board.py 40-55 ===

Usage:
  check-board.py                              push mode: validate the repo's real WAITING.md (b and c).
  check-board.py --board FILE                 validate one board file (b and c).
  check-board.py --board FILE --report FILE   also check the closing report omits no open item (a).
"""
import argparse
import os
import re

      PS       = "(^|[^a-zA-Z._])ps([^a-zA-Z]|$)"                 # a `ps` listing, the other resolver

=== 536edac ===
536edac1f4fb72814ded061ef7ade1dfb0556c67
2026-07-28
Every live document is measured, and the readability work gets a written plan
scripts/rule-census.py runs three readings over every live document: prose sentences
past rule r08's word cap read out of the rule home, the style lint at its full tier, and
the register lint. 106 files, 5429 findings — 2286 at the top level, 1712 in the skill
bodies, 1104 under docs/. The counts land in guardrails/rule-census.json as the limit
that only falls.

The sentence splitter reads a list item and a `**field** — value` line as its own unit.
Joining them the way wrapped prose is joined once read a block of label lines in
ARCHITECTURE.md as one sentence of 1914 words.

docs/plans/2026-07-28-top-level-readability.md is the plan the next session executes
from a clean context: the goal as a test on ONE requirement, why the 2026-07-27 loop did
not converge, the seven rules with their measures, a machine for the rule readers
actually stop on, the batch loop with five self-checks, a pilot that reports before the
rest is committed to, an honest account of what this seat can and cannot do, and the
plan's own weaknesses.

26ea15e820c8c47fe47f330e84f00940adf3d4d4

twelve fresh workers over the accepted 15-code gold sample, register-linted, and cleared by a
fresh-seat adversarial audit (INV-237) that blocked on a wrong growth figure and two accuracy nits,
all folded. Version stamped 3.0.0 across skills and the plugin manifest. Suite 1651 green.

The last of the row-420 gate-audit's four members. At a stopping point the run
reports a runaway descendant it provably owns — what it is, how much of a core it
holds, and why the run owns it (Alexander 2026-07-17 ~16:58, the notice word that
